query: For phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys, what single intervention could improve glass-forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state? Formulate one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention without presupposing its class, the mechanism by which it would act, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise comparable baseline, the conditions under which it should or should not work, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the configurational complexity by adding one additional principal element (while maintaining the phosphorus level) improves both the glass‐forming ability and the thermal stability of the amorphous state in phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: A phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy (or compositionally complex) alloy with a baseline set of principal metallic elements processed into an amorphous phase (e.g., via rapid quenching).
generation.intervention: Introduce one extra principal element to increase the overall compositional complexity without altering the phosphorus content.
generation.conditions: This intervention should be effective if the added element has a sufficiently different atomic size and favorable mixing enthalpy such that it enhances atomic-level disorder without promoting phase separation or unwanted crystalline phases. It is expected to work under processing conditions (e.g., melt quenching) that inherently support amorphization and should not work if the new element instead acts as a nucleation site for crystallization.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased degree of atomic disorder and a broader distribution of local chemical environments that raise kinetic and thermodynamic barriers to crystallization.
generation.mechanism: The addition boosts the configurational entropy and accentuates the atomic size mismatch. This creates a more energetically and kinetically stable amorphous state by hindering nucleation and growth of crystals, thus extending the temperature window of the supercooled liquid and delaying crystallization.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a baseline alloy without the intervention, the modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a higher onset temperature of crystallization, an extended supercooled liquid region, and greater critical casting thickness indicative of an improved glass‐forming ability and enhanced thermal stability.
generation.baseline: Phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloys with the original, fewer principal elements processed under similar rapid solidification conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is likely contingent on the specific choice and concentration of the additional element. If the new element does not create a significant atomic size or bonding contrast, or if it induces segregation or unwanted secondary phases, the beneficial effect may be absent or even detrimental.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvement in glass‐forming ability and thermal stability is uncertain and will depend strongly on the selected additional element and its proportion in the alloy. Optimization of these parameters is required to realize the intended effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of phosphorus‐containing high‐entropy alloy samples using identical melt-quenching conditions: one set with the baseline composition and one set with the additional principal element introduced to increase configurational entropy. Perform differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to locate the glass transition temperature (Tg) and the crystallization onset temperature (Tx) as indicators of thermal stability. Complement these tests with critical casting thickness measurements and structural characterizations using X-ray diffraction (XRD) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
measurements: Glass transition temperature (Tg) and onset of crystallization (Tx) using DSC
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy with the additional principal element does not show a statistically significant enhancement in Tx, ΔTx, and critical casting thickness—indicating no improvement in glass‐forming ability and thermal stability relative to the baseline—or if it exhibits new crystalline phases or unfavorable microstructure, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Decoupling between calorimetric and dynamical glass transitions in high-entropy metallic glasses

Abstract: Glass transition is one of the unresolved critical issues in solid-state physics and materials science, during which a viscous liquid is frozen into a solid or structurally arrested state. On account of the uniform arrested mechanism, the calorimetric glass transition temperature (Tg) always follows the same trend as the dynamical glass transition (or α-relaxation) temperature (Tα) determined by dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA). Here, we explored the correlations between the calorimetric and dynamical glass transitions of three prototypical high-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs) systems. We found that the HEMGs present a depressed dynamical glass transition phenomenon, i.e., HEMGs with moderate calorimetric Tg represent the highest Tα and the maximum activation energy of α-relaxation. High-entropy induced a glass-to-glass transition in a metallic glass

Abstract: AbstractGlass-to-glass transitions are useful for us to understand the glass nature, but it remains difficult to tune the metallic glass into significantly different glass states. Here, we have demonstrated that the high-entropy can enhance the degree of disorder in an equiatomic high-entropy metallic glass NbNiZrTiCo and elevate it to a high-energy glass state. An unusual glass-to-glass phase transition is discovered during heating with an enormous heat release even larger than that of the following crystallization at higher temperatures. Dramatic atomic rearrangement with a short- and medium-range ordering is revealed by in-situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction analyses. This glass-to-glass transition leads to a significant improvement in the modulus, hardness, and thermal stability, all of which could promote their applications. Based on the proposed high-entropy effect, two high-entropy metallic glasses are developed and they show similar glass-to-glass transitions. These findings uncover a high-entropy effect in metallic glasses and create a pathway for tuning the glass states and properties.Subject t
